case_name: Mason v Mansion House Estates Ltd.
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Mason v. Mansion House Estates Ltd.,

2021 BCSC 2465

Date: 20211220

Docket:
S216918

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

Robert
Mason

Plaintiff

And

Mansion
House Estates Ltd., Carol Ciprut, Frank Eberlein, Nancy Higgs, Dorothy Keung,
Louis Klessens also known as Lou Klessens, Patrick Le Cefr, Catherine Oi Ying
So, Shiela Wenzel, John Doe I, John Doe II, John Doe III and John Doe IV

Defendants

-
and -

Docket:
S198446

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

The
Mansion House Estates Ltd.

Petitioner

And

Robert
C. Mason

Respondent

Corrected Judgment: The text of the judgment was corrected on July
4, 2022

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Schultes

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff, in Action No:
S216918 and Respondent, in Action No: S198446:

Kang
Yang

Counsel for Defendants, in Action No.
S216918:

Steven
W. Lesiuk

Counsel for The Mansion House Estates Ltd.,
Petitioner in Action No. S198446:

Jean-Kyle
R. Bienvenu

Ashleigh
K. Hall

Place and Date of Hearing:

New
Westminster, B.C.

February
21, 2020

January
29, 2021

Place and Date of Judgment:

New
Westminster, B.C.

December
20, 2021

Introduction

[
1
]

These applications arise in the course of a
dispute between Mansion House Estates Ltd., a business corporation that
operates an apartment building in Vancouver in which its shareholders are
entitled to reside, and Robert Mason, who is one of its shareholders and the
leaseholder of a specific unit.

[
2
]

In New Westminster S216918, Mansion House is
applying to strike Mr. Mason’s most recent notice of civil claim against
it and numerous personal defendants
[1]

who are involved in its operation. In turn, Mr. Mason is applying to have the
action that was commenced by that notice of civil claim heard together with a
petition that Mansion House has brought against him as Vancouver S198446, with
the petition being converted to an action and put on the trial list for that purpose.
He also seeks a waiver of the implied undertaking with respect to the previous
actions between the parties, which were settled.

Background

[
3
]

Although Mansion House resembles a strata
corporation in its functioning, it is incorporated under the provincial
Business
Corporations Act (“BCA”)
, and is subject to the usual governance of a
business corporation. Its shareholders are also leaseholders of particular
units in the building. Occupancy is governed by an agreement among the
shareholders known as the “House Rules”, which are then enforced by the
corporation. It is open to the shareholders and directors to vote to end the
tenancy of a shareholder. That occurred with respect to Mr. Mason’s tenancy in
2019.

[
4
]

Mr. Mason purchased his shares in Mansion House
and entered into the lease for his unit in 2000. A dispute arose between him
and Mansion House about a solarium and a shed on his unit’s rooftop patio,
which Mansion House wished to remove. This dispute led to several court
actions, and to the imposition of fines and other sanctions on Mr. Mason by
Mansion House.

[
5
]

In 2018, the parties entered into a settlement
agreement that was intended to resolve the two previous actions brought by Mr.
Mason and a previous petition that had been brought by Mansion House. There was
also a consent dismissal of those proceedings. Mr. Mason says that he complied
with his obligations under the agreement but that Mansion House, contrary to an
implied term of it, continued to harass him. He filed the notice of civil claim
that is in issue in this application in 2019. It was drafted by his previous
counsel. Mansion House then filed its petition pursuant to s.19 of the
Commercial
Tenancy Act
[
“CTA”
], seeking to end his tenancy.

[
6
]

Following an application on September 30, 2019, Justice
Skolrood set a hearing pursuant to section 19 of the
CTA
“to determine
whether [Mr. Mason] holds possession against the right of [Mansion House] and
whether [Mr. Mason] has wrongfully refused to go out of possession, having no
right to continue in possession…”. Such an order is to be made under that
section when “it appears to the court [on the basis of an affidavit filed by
the petitioner] that the tenant wrongfully holds and the landlord is entitled
to possession”, at which point he will set a hearing to determine the matters
referred to in the order.

[
7
]

During the hearing of the present applications,
Mr. Mason’s counsel provided a draft amended notice of civil claim. It removes
the claims for defamation and abuse of process that are found in the existing
notice, deletes certain passages and entire paragraphs, reorganizes order of the
paragraphs, and adds additional facts in support of the claims. His counsel had
not yet filed at the time of the applications because Mansion House’s counsel
still objected to it in its amended form, and he did not wish to waste his single
opportunity under the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
to amend it without
leave, when it was going be subject to an application to strike in any event.

[
8
]

Despite it not being filed, Mansion House’s
counsel agreed that I could consider this draft notice when deciding whether
the objectionable portions of the current one are capable of being amended, and
in particular whether Mr. Mason has still failed to plead some of the claims
correctly in his second attempt.

Striking Parts of the Notice of
Civil Claim

General Principles

[
9
]

The relevant portions of
Rule
9-5
provide:

(1)        At any stage of a proceeding, the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it discloses no reasonable claim
or defence, as the case may be,

(b)        it is unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it may prejudice, embarrass or
delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d)        it is otherwise an abuse of the
process of the court,

and the court may pronounce judgment or
order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the
application to be paid as special costs.

(2)        No
evidence is admissible on an application under subrule (1) (a).

[
10
]

It is also worth noting that
Rule
3-1(2)
provides, in part:

(2)        A notice of civil claim must do
the following:

(a)        set out a concise statement of
the material facts giving rise to the claim;

(b)        set out the relief sought by the
plaintiff against each named defendant;

(c)        set out a concise summary of the
legal basis for the relief sought…

[
11
]

For the purposes of this application, there is no real dispute about
the meaning of these provisions.

[
12
]

Dealing first with applications pursuant to 9-5(1)(a)
Justice Fisher explained in
Willow v. Chong
,
2013
BCSC 1083

that:

[18]      The
test for striking a claim as disclosing no reasonable claim under Rule 9
‑
5(1)(a), set out in
Hunt v Carey Canada Inc
.,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 SCR
959 and reiterated more recently in
R. v Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd
.,

2011 SCC 42
, is whether it is “plain and obvious,” assuming the facts pleaded
are true, that the claim discloses no reasonable cause of action, has no
reasonable prospect of success, or if the action is “certain to fail.” If there
is a chance that the plaintiffs might succeed, then they should not be “driven
from the judgment seat.”...

[
13
]

This analysis includes a consideration of the pleadings as they
might be amended:
Kripps v. Touche Ross & Co.,
(1992)
1992 CanLII 923 (BC CA)
, 69 B.C.L.R.
(2d) 62 at para.68.

[
14
]

In
FORCOMP Forestry Consulting Ltd. v.
British Columbia
,
2021 BCCA 465
, Justice Voith summarized some additional
key points:

[21]      … In
McNaughton v. Baker

(1988), 25 B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 at 25,
1988 CanLII 3036 (C.A.)
, the Court said that
in order to strike out a pleading on the ground that it discloses no reasonable
cause of action the case must be “perfectly clear”. In…
Imperial Tobacco

Canada
…at
paras. 19–20, the Court said that R. 9
‑
5(1)(a), or its
predecessor provision, served the “valuable housekeeping measure” of weeding
out “hopeless claims” from those that have “some chance of success”.

[22]      The
authorities are also consistent in directing that a court, on an application to
strike a statement of claim as disclosing no reasonable cause of action, is
required to read the statement of claim generously and to accommodate
inadequacies in form that are merely the result of drafting deficiencies:
Nevsun
Resources Ltd. v. Araya
,
2020 SCC 5
at para.
143
;
British Columbia/Yukon
Association of Drug War Survivors v. Abbotsford (City)
,
2015 BCCA 142
at
para.
15
;
Thompson v. Webber
,
2010 BCCA 308
at para.
41
, leave to appeal
to SCC ref’d, 33825 (23 December 2010).

[
15
]

As Voith J.A. further explained:

[25]      For a
cause of action to be properly advanced, the elements of the cause of action
must be set out, the material facts that ground those various elements of the
cause of action must be concisely stated, and the relief that is sought must be
available for the specific cause of action advanced.

[
16
]

Voith J.A. cited the explanation of what constitutes
a material fact in
Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies Inc.
,
2001 SCC 44
, in
which Justice Binnie said that:

54        A
cause of action has traditionally been defined as comprising every fact which
it would be necessary for the plaintiff to prove, if disputed, in order to
support his or her right to the judgment of the court:
Poucher v. Wilkins

(1915),
1915 CanLII 514 (ON CA)
, 33 O.L.R. 125 (C.A.). Establishing each such fact (sometimes referred
to as material facts) constitutes a precondition to success. It is apparent
that different causes of action may have one or more material facts in common…

[
17
]

Pleadings may be struck on this basis with or without leave being
given to amend them.

[
18
]

With respect to 9-5(1)(b), Fisher J. explained
in
Willow
that:

[20]      … a
pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to establishing the
plaintiff's cause of action, if it does not advance any claim known in law,
where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it would serve no
useful purpose and would be a waste of the court's time and public resources:
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No.
2160 (SC (in chambers));
Skender v. Farley
,
2007 BCCA 629
. [at para. 20
(CanLII)]

[
19
]

This reasoning was cited by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Nevsun

at para.65.

[
20
]

As to 9-5(1)(c), Justice Forth set out the
requirements for its application  in
Grosz v. Royal Trust Corp. of Canada
,

2020 BCSC 128
:

64        Under
R. 9-5(1)(c), a pleading is "embarrassing" where it is so irrelevant
that it will involve the parties in useless expense or where the pleadings are
so confusing that it is difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C.
(4th) 266 (S.C.) at para.
47
. A pleading is prejudicial where it fails to
identify the cause of action, contains irrelevant material, or is intended to
confuse:
Camp Development Corporation v. Greater Vancouver (Transportation
Authority)
,
2009 BCSC 819
at para.
27
, aff'd
2010 BCCA 284
.

[
21
]

Fisher J. also addressed the requirements for
striking a claim for an abuse of process under 9-5(1)(d) in
Willow
:

[21]      Abuse
of process under Rule 9
‑
(5)(1)(d) or the court’s inherent discretion is a flexible doctrine.
It allows the court to prevent a claim from proceeding where to do so would
violate principles of judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity
of the administration of justice...A claim may…be struck as an abuse of process
where it is an attempt to re
‑
litigate an issue that has already been decided …

[
22
]

Finally,
Mercantile Office Systems Private
Ltd. v. Worldwide Warranty Life Services Inc.,
2021 BCCA 362
offers a
helpful overview of the correct approach to drafting pleadings, which in turn
assists in assessing their sufficiency. Addressing the chambers judge’s
assertion that a pleading is a “factual narrative”, Voith J.A. explained:

[43]      Once again, elements of the
judge's assertions are accurate. Drafting a pleading is not a mathematical
exercise. It involves the exercise of judgment and it requires some degree of
flexibility. This is reflected, for example, in R. 22-3(1) [which allows the
required forms for filing pleadings to contain “variations as the circumstances
of the proceeding require”] and in the numerous decisions where judges have
considered the adequacy of a pleading. In addition, R. 1-1(2) confirms that,
unless a contrary intention appears, the
Interpretation Act
, R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 238, applies to the
Rules
. Section 8 of the
Act
confirms
that every enactment is to be construed as remedial and be given such
"fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures
the attainment of its objects."

[44]
Nevertheless, none of a notice
of claim, a response to civil claim, and a counterclaim is a story. Each pleading
contemplates and requires a reasonably disciplined exercise that is governed,
in many instances in mandatory terms, by the
Rules
and the relevant
authorities.
Each requires the drafting party to "concisely" set
out the "material facts" that give rise to the claim or that relate
to the matters raised by the claim. None of these pleadings are permitted to
contain evidence or argument.

[Emphasis added]

Positions

Mansion House

[
23
]

The first concern expressed by Mansion House is with respect to
paragraphs 14 to 40 of the current notice of civil claim. Under the heading of
“Procedural History” the notice sets out Mr. Mason’s characterizations of the
parties’ disputes since 2001, ending with in the filing of a petition by
Mansion House in 2017. Paragraph 41 then sets out the terms of the settlement
agreement that resolved the outstanding proceedings.

[
24
]

Mansion House submits that these paragraphs leading up to the
description of the settlement agreement are an abuse of process, because they
seek to rely on events that are
res judicata
as a result of the
settlement agreement and the consent dismissal of all of the proceedings. Even
if, as Mr. Mason indicates in his application response, these events have been
set out in the notice only for the purposes of providing context, and to show
the measure of damages that should flow from a breach of the settlement
agreement, and even if none of the causes of action currently being pursued
depend on them, they are still irrelevant, embarrassing, scandalous, and
vexatious as those terms have been defined in the authorities cited above, and
should be struck. In the case of the damages for the breach, that is because
the measure of damages will be the amount needed to put Mr. Mason in the same
position as if the agreement had been complied with – an analysis that does not
depend on the procedural history.

[
25
]

A further practical problem is that if the implied undertaking with
respect to the previous actions is waived, as Mr. Mason seeks in the companion
application, Mansion House could find itself having to produce 17 years’ worth
of documents that are irrelevant to the present claims.

[
26
]

Turning to the specific causes of action, Mansion House asks that
the claims for defamation and abuse of process, which have been deleted from
the amended notice, be struck from the current one. Counsel also notes that
while there is a reference in the “Legal Basis” section of the notice to the
“disparity of power” between the parties creating a fiduciary duty on Mansion
House’s part towards Mr. Mason, no material facts have been pleaded in
support of such a duty, and in his application response Mr. Mason does not list
it as one of the claims he is pursuing in the draft amended notice. As a
result, Mansion House submits that it should be struck as well.

[
27
]

The claims that Mr. Mason says in the application response that he
is still pursuing are for breach of the settlement agreement, oppression,
trespass and conspiracy.

[
28
]

The problem with the breach allegation, according to Mansion House,
is that two of the three breaches alleged in the “Statement of Facts” section are
not based on actual terms of the settlement agreement. Mr. Mason alleges that
Mansion House failed to complete repairs to the roof, whereas it was only
required to use its “best efforts” to do so, by a specified date. What is worse,
its alleged breach by failing to repair the patio “to the quality it was prior
to the commencement of the renovation work” is not supported by any term of the
agreement. (Mansion House accepts that the third breach does relate to a
specific term, and can remain.) Lastly under this heading, there is no mention
of any damages flowing from the breaches, which is a required element.

[
29
]

The first difficulty with the oppression claim that Mansion house
identifies is that Mr. Mason has set out particulars of what is described as
Mansion House’s “oppressive and
wrongful conduct
”. It is not specified
whether the wrongful aspect relates to the oppression claim, or one of the
others. In view of the number of different participants that Mr. Mason has
taken action against, his general lack of care in supporting his claims, and
the fact that these paragraphs in the draft amended claim are used in the
current notice to support the breach of the settlement agreement, this wording
is said to introduce an unacceptable level of uncertainty.

[
30
]

A more basic problem is that s. 227 of the
Business Corporations
Act
requires an oppression remedy to be sought by means of a petition
(although there is provision in the
Rules
for a petition to be converted
to an action in appropriate circumstances.) If the oppression claim is allowed
to stand despite this procedural obstacle, Mansion House submits that it must then
be pleaded “with some degree of precision”.

[
31
]

The trespass claim is based on the allegation that a member of the
Mansion House board “took steps to enter [Mr. Mason’s unit], or otherwise spoof
a call from the plaintiff’s phone number and call the 9-1-1 emergency line”,
resulting in police attendance. Mansion House points out that it is not alleged
that one of the defendants actually entered the unit, which is contrary to the
requirements that a trespass be direct, intentional or negligent and physical (
Shaman
v. Meek
,
2019 BCSC 9
at para.131, citing
Philip H. Osborne, The Law of
Torts
, 4th ed. (Toronto: Irwin Law, 2011) at 296-298). Thus, this claim is
unsupported by the required material facts.

[
32
]

The further difficulty created by this claim is with respect to the
numerous named personal defendants in the current notice of civil claim.
[2]

Quite aside from being unable to assert that anyone actually entered his unit,
there is no basis on which any of the named defendants can determine what they
are supposed to have done. Adding to this confusion, the trespass is alleged to
have been committed by “the Board of [Mansion House] or one of its agents”. In
this regard, counsel reminds me of the admonition of Chief Justice McLachlin at
para. 22 of
R. v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
,
2011 SCC 42 (CanLII)
, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 45 that,
whether or not a plaintiff is in a position to prove the facts that give rise
to liability at the time they file their notice of civil claim, it is still
required to plead such facts.

[
33
]

The last claim is with respect to conspiracy. While here are no
facts alleged to support it in the current notice, the draft amended notice
contains two paragraphs under that heading. They allege that (1) Mansion House
implemented house rules that it knew Mr. Mason would have difficulty complying
with, because of conditions that Mansion House itself had created; and (2) “in
particular” two named shareholders worked “in concert” to misrepresent facts to
other shareholders, so that the other shareholders would oppose Mr. Mason’s
application to the Vancouver Board of Variance for permission to build a new
solarium, which failed as a result.

[
34
]

Mansion House submits that neither of the ways
in which this tort can be established – the so-called “simple motive” and
“unlawful conduct” conspiracies – are supported by these facts, including the
requirement that damages were caused by the defendants’ conduct. To demonstrate
the required elements that are missing here, counsel relied on the summary of
the law that was provided by Justice Williams in
Alexis v. Drury
,
2017
BCSC 674
, which included this helpful passage from
Harris v. GlaxoSmithKline
Inc
.,
2010 ONSC 2326
,

[74]      In
Canada, the tort of conspiracy can be committed in two discrete ways that may
arise on the same set of facts; namely, (1) by two or more persons using some
means (lawful or unlawful) for the predominate purpose of injuring the
plaintiff; and (2) by two or more persons using unlawful means with knowledge
that their acts were aimed at the plaintiff and knowing or constructively
knowing that their acts would result in injury to the plaintiff. The other elements
of the tort of conspiracy are: (a) an agreement to injure between two or more
persons; (b) acts in furtherance of the agreement to injure; and (c) the
plaintiff suffering damages as a result of the defendants' conduct.

[
35
]

In addition to these deficiencies in the specific causes of action,
Mansion House argues that paragraphs 1-5 and 8-11 of the “Legal Basis” are
essentially argument, and should be struck on that basis

Mr. Mason

[
36
]

In overview, he stresses the “generous and non-technical” approach
that should be taken to amendments that “are necessary to determine the real
question between the parties, considering always the interests of justice”:
Century
Services Inc. v. LeRoy,
2015 BCCA 120
at para.
10
. Any identified
deficiencies in the pleadings should be addressed with those principles in
mind.

[
37
]

He does not accept that there was no basis for the abuse of process
and defamation that are omitted from the draft amended notice. He emphasizes
that he has simply chosen not to maintain them.

[
38
]

As Mansion House’s submissions anticipated, he argues that the
paragraphs preceding the description of the settlement agreement provide
necessary context, without which the terms of the settlement and the manner in
which it was breached would not be comprehensible. With respect to any of his
claims being
res judicata
because of the settlement and the consent
dismissals, he stresses that all the actual claims in this notice arise from
actions by Mansion House that post-date those events.

[
39
]

As to the alleges breaches themselves, he submits that Mansion House’s
failure to complete the roof repairs clearly includes the term of the agreement
that it “use all best efforts” to complete them by a date that has since
passed.

[
40
]

Mansion House’s argument that his reference to “wrongful” conduct in
conjunction with the oppression claim causes confusion is unsustainable, Mr.
Mason points out, in light of the definition of oppressive conduct as that
which is “burdensome, harsh or wrongful”:
Walker et al. v. Betts et al.
,

2006 BCSC 128
at para.
80
. In other words, I took it, there could be no other
possible type of conduct to which “wrongful” could be understood to refer to.

[
41
]

While acknowledging that oppression claims are “typically” brought
by petition, Mr. Mason notes that if he had done that there would then be three
outstanding proceedings, and the oppression claim actually overlaps with the
trespass and conspiracy claims that are properly part of this action, in that
they all arise from the undermining of efforts to build a new solarium. In those
circumstances it would be impractical to require him to commence a petition,
only to apply to have it consolidated with the other two. He refers to the
decision in
Madco Investments Ltd. v. Western Tank & Lining Ltd.
,
2017 BCSCC 219 at para. 53, where it was noted that “the
Rules

themselves expressly contemplate occasions on which matters raised in a
petition may be more appropriately resolved by way of a trial (Rule
22-1(7)(d))…” and that it was not necessary in that case “to superimpose on the
Claim the procedural requirements (and limitations) that are ordinarily
attached to a petition.”(However, I note that in that case the opposing parties
had withdrawn their application to strike the oppression claim on the basis
that it should have been brought as a petition.)

[
42
]

With respect to the trespass claim, Mr. Mason says that it is taking
issue with “semantics” to focus on the words “took steps to” in relation to the
entry of his property for the 911 call and argue that there are no facts
pleaded that constitute the required physical entry. If necessary, those words
could simply be deleted. And while the reference to spoofing might well support
some other claim, the part of the relevant paragraph that alleges a trespass is
complete as currently pleaded.

[
43
]

Turning to the conspiracy, Mr. Mason submits that all of the
elements of the “lawful act” variety of conspiracy have been properly pleaded
here, arising from the attempts of the two specific shareholders and the board
of directors generally in opposing the new solarium. The very background facts
that Mansion House says should be deleted show clearly the importance of the
solarium to him, and that interference with his ability to build it would cause
significant injury to him.

[
44
]

As to the failure to name other specific defendants and their roles,
beyond the two named shareholders involved in the conspiracy, he explains that it
is “not really practical” for him to name every individual defendant as a
co-tortfeasor.

Discussion

[
45
]

First of all, I will base my consideration of the adequacy of Mr.
Mason’s pleadings on the draft amended notice, since it represents his most
recent efforts to present his claims. I do not agree with Mansion House,
however, that any remaining deficiencies should necessarily be struck without
leave to amend because this is his second attempt at pleading them correctly.
That question is still to be resolved based on whether the amended notice
discloses claims that are capable of amendment, whether or not that has been attempted
so far.

[
46
]

I agree with Mansion House that the majority of the “Procedural
History” section serves no useful purpose in advancing the current claims.
While it was necessary in order to understand the allegations arising from the
settlement agreement to know that disputes between Mr. Mason and Mansion House
about the solarium and the shed led to the three proceedings that were the
resolved by the agreement, these paragraphs go well beyond that necessary
background, to revisit those disputes in considerable detail, and in language
that would be leave one with the impression that they relate to active claims.
As a result, they are more than a harmless irrelevance – they are an active
distraction from the essential focus on the material facts of the actual claims
in issue. One could describe them as irrelevant, scandalous or embarrassing as
those terms have been defined in the cases. Accordingly, paragraphs 14 to 40
are struck, with leave to amend by replacing them with a concise description of
the existence of the dispute, its subject matter, and the fact that it resulted
in the three proceedings.

[
47
]

On the breach of the settlement agreement itself, I cannot accept
Mr. Mason’s argument that the assertion that Mansion House failed to complete
the roof repairs necessarily includes a failure to use its best efforts to do
so. Therefore, sub-paragraph (43(a)) is struck with leave to amend to allege a
breach that is based on the language of the agreement. His counsel did not
address sub-paragraph 43(b) – the failure to repair the patio to its previous
quality - in his submissions, which I took to be an acknowledgment that there
was no term, express or implied, requiring Mansion House to do so. It will also
be struck, but without leave to amend.

[
48
]

Finally under this heading, it is incorrect to assert, as Mansion
House does, that the paragraphs alleging the breaches do not indicate that
damages flowed from them. The consequences of each breach are described in their
respective paragraphs, which link clearly enough with the claim for damages arising
from them under “Relief Sought”. I would not have struck any of them on that
basis.

[
49
]

The inclusion of “wrongful” in the heading of the oppression section
is unnecessary – the wrong in question does not have to be defined legally in
the “Statement of Facts”- and given the rather vague manner in which some of
the claims are raised it could well cause confusion in framing an appropriate
response. It will be struck, without leave to amend.

[
50
]

More fundamentally, Mr. Mason has advanced no real basis other than
convenience to include the oppression claim in this action. If that were sufficient,
there would be little need for
Rule
22-1(7). In fact, an application to
have a trial of a petition pursuant to the
Rule
is not a foregone
conclusion, depending as it does on the identification of “bona fide triable
issues” of fact or law, unless the applicant is “bound to lose”:
British
Columbia (Milk Marketing Board) v Saputo Products Canada G.P./ Saputo Produits
Laitiers Canada S.E.N.C.
,
2017 BCCA 247
at paras.
45-46
. It is not appropriate
to anticipate the outcome of such an application in the course of deciding the
present one, and proportionality, important as it is, is not a licence to
circumvent legislative requirements. Accordingly, paras. 44-47 are struck, with
leave to bring them in the form of a petition, except for subparagraphs
44.f.-j., which are relied on in support of the trespass claim.

[
51
]

Those trespass allegations are sufficient as pleaded. To say that a board
member or one of their agents “took steps” to enter Mr. Mason’s unit is not as
direct a description as one might prefer, but it does not undermine the basic
assertion that one of them physically entered. Mr. Mason has chosen to add the
alternative that his phone number was “spoofed” (which I take notice refers to
a practice of using one phone number to imitate a call from another), an
allegation that is not currently grounded in any recognized tort, but that is a
self-regulating deficiency, in the sense that if he fails to prove physical
entry as a conventional trespass the claim will not be made out
[3]
. I do not see how its
inclusion could confuse Mansion House in its response.

[
52
]

The conspiracy claims are also adequate in their present form. It
would be preferable to amend paragraph 48 – in which “the [d]efendants” are
said to have “proposed and implemented” House Rules that Mr. Mason could not
comply with – to explicitly assert that they agreed to carry out that action
against him, but I think that is sufficiently implied by the role the personal
defendants in Mansion House’s governance, which necessarily operates by means
of the directors’ and shareholders’ actions. I would not strike it on that
basis.

[
53
]

The allegation of the two particular named defendants working in
concert to thwart approval of the solarium in paragraph 49. is also
sufficiently clear as pleaded.

[
54
]

Further, the damages alleged to have resulted to Mr. Mason from each
agreement seem obvious, and clearly arise from the language used in their
respective paragraphs: being set up for needless rule violations in para. 48,
and being unable to rebuild his solarium in para. 49.

[
55
]

As to Mansion House’s confusion about which personal defendants are
alleged to have committed each of the relevant acts, I think that this is a
function of a larger problem in the draft amended notice. It specifically names
only the two shareholders who are said to have engaged in the second conspiracy
as parties, along with “the Board of Directors” of Mansion House, which is not
a separate legal entity. Within the notice itself it lists the members of the
“present board of directors” (who are named individually as parties in the
current notice) without making it clear whether they were its members at the
material times. It then describes the four John Doe defendants as “members of
[Mansion House], agents of these members or other people who have contributed
to the wrongful conduct against the plaintiff…”

[
56
]

This is not a correct approach. There is nothing wrong with being
unable to say which members of a group of named defendants participated in a
specific act, as long as there is some basis to connect each of them with it.
There is also nothing wrong with naming a John Doe defendant to represent a
person who engaged in tortious acts but whose identity is not known. However, this
pleading conflates these two distinct kinds of defendant. Further compounding
this problem, the pleading uses “the Defendants” “MHE” (Mansion House), “the
Board” seemingly interchangeably, in addition to the “member of the Board of
MHE or one of its agents” who are alleged to have committed the trespass, and
the two named shareholders who are alleged to have fomented opposition to the
new solarium.

[
57
]

I will not strike the balance of the notice on this basis however,
because the existing one naming the board members individually at least leaves
open the possibility that they are being held liable in their personal
capacities, and that their actions also underlie the liability of Mansion
House. Mr. Mason would be well advised to address the lack of clarity
surrounding this issue in whatever amended notice is eventually filed.

[
58
]

Next, while the draft amended notice has removed some of the
impugned paragraphs from the “Legal Basis” section, paragraphs 1-3 and 11
remain. They seek to persuade the reader that Mansion House should not:

•

Have its petition remedy before Mr. Mason’s
claims have been adjudicated;

•

Be able to shield itself behind the implied
undertaking;

•

Take advantage of its status as a business
corporation; or

•

Rely on a settlement agreement that it
intentionally breached.

These paragraphs are pure argument, and do
nothing to fulfil the intended purpose of the section. They are struck, with
leave to file replacement paragraphs that properly address the legal basis of
the remedies that are being sought.

[
59
]

Finally, I would not strike the abuse of process and defamation
claims that Mr. Mason says he is not proceeding with and has deleted from
the draft notice, or the breach of fiduciary duty claim that is referred to in
the amended notice but was not addressed in the application response or in
submissions. I think it is appropriate to accept his counsel’s submissions that
he does not intend to rely on them. If they resurface in any future applications
to amend they can be dealt with on their merits at that point.

Converting Mansion’s House’s
Petition to an Action and Hearing it with Mr. Mason’s Action

General Principles

Ordering a Petition to the Trial
List

[
60
]

As I have indicated in relation to the previous
application, the governing authority on this issue is the decision of the Court
of Appeal in
Saputo
, which held:

[44]      In
Robertson
[
v. Dhillon
,

2015 BCCA 469
], the Court set out the test to determine whether a petition
should be converted to a trial:

[55]      On the hearing of a petition, a
judge must be satisfied that there is no dispute as to the facts or law which
raises a reasonable doubt or which suggests that there is a defence that
deserves to be tried:
Douglas Lake Cattle Co. v. Smith
(1991),
1991 CanLII 3954 (BC CA)
, 54
B.C.L.R. (2d) 52 (C.A.) at 59. If such a dispute exists, the judge may refer
the matter to the trial list, pursuant to R. 22-1(7) (former R. 52(11)(d)).

[56] The test is not that used to determine
a summary trial. Rather it is akin to that on an application for summary
judgment under R. 9-6. Mr. Justice Lambert summarized the task in
Montroyal
Estates Ltd. v. D.J.C.A. Investments Ltd
. (1984),
1984 CanLII 775 (BC CA)
, 55 B.C.L.R. 137 (C.A.) at
138-39:

We were referred by counsel for T & A
Holdings Ltd. to the judgment of Esson J. (as he then was) in
Progressive
Const. Ltd. v. Newton
,
1980 CanLII 493 (BC SC)
, 25 B.C.L.R. 330, [1981] 2 W.W.R. 741, 117 D.L.R.
(3d) 591 (S.C.), and particularly at p. 334. There Esson J. summarizes, in my
opinion, accurately, the law in relation to establishing a defence on an
application for summary judgment in these words [pp. 334-35]:

The cases do not establish an invariable
rule as to what steps must be taken to resist a R. 18 application for summary
judgment.
On all such applications the issue is whether, on the relevant
facts and applicable law, there is a bona fide triable issue.
The onus of
establishing that there is not such an issue rests upon the applicant, and must
be carried to the point of making it "manifestly clear", which I take
to mean much the same as beyond a reasonable doubt. If the judge hearing the
application is left in doubt as to whether there is a triable issue, the
application should be dismissed.

In essence, if the defendant is bound to
lose, the application should be granted, but if he is not bound to lose, then
the application should be dismissed.

[Emphasis added.]

[46]      …[A]s noted in
Robertson
,
the test for determining whether a matter should be converted into an action is
not that used to determine suitability for a summary trial, but rather is akin
to that on application for summary judgment under Rule 9-6. The suggestion in
Boffo
[Boffo Developments (Jewel 2) Ltd. v. Pinnacle International (Wilson) Plaza
Inc.
,
2009 BCSC 1701
] that the mere existence of a
bona fide
triable
issue is not in itself sufficient to warrant conversion to the trial list is,
with respect, contrary to the test for converting a matter to an action
established in this Court.

[47]      I
would note the fact that a matter is converted to an action does not
necessarily mean that a full trial will be required. It still remains open to
the parties to bring a summary trial application under Rule 9-7.

Hearing Trials Together

[
61
]

These principles were summarized by Justice
MacDonald in
Raymond James Investment Counsel Ltd. v. Clyne
,
2018 BCSC
720
:

[36]      In
Hui v. Hoa
,
2012 BCSC
1045 (B.C. S.C.)
[
Hui
], Master MacNaughton (as she then was) outlined
the law regarding joinders:

[33]      The law with respect to when two
proceedings should be tried together was helpfully summarized by Master Shaw in

Egan v. ICBC
,
2010 BCSC 1042
. Briefly, there are two questions which
must be answered. The first involves considering whether the two proceedings
involve common claims, disputes and relationships. As set out in
Merritt v.
Imasco Enterprises Inc.
,
(1992) 2 C.P.C. (3d) 275
, that determination is
made on a review of the pleadings.

[34]      The second question is whether
the two proceedings are so interwoven as to make separate trials at different
times before different judges undesirable and fraught with problems and
expense. This question involves considering a number of factors including
whether trial together will:

a)         create a saving in pre-trial
procedures;

b)         reduce the number of trial days;

c)         seriously inconvenience a party
by being required to attend part of a joined proceeding in which they may have
little or no interest;

[35]      Other factors to be considered
are whether:

a)         one of the proceedings is at a
more advanced stage than the other;

b)         trial together will result in a
delay of the trial of one of the proceedings and the prejudice of that delay
outweighing the potential benefits of trial together;

c)         there is a risk of inconsistent
findings on identical issues; and

d)         one party might be deprived of
their right to a jury trial.

[38]      When considering joining actions,
the court must determine whether the degree of commonality and intertwining of
issues outweighs the prejudicial factors raised by the party opposing the
order:
Simmonds v. Victoria (City)
,
2016 BCSC 951
(B.C.S.C.) at para.

25
;
Liu
at para. 4.

[39]      An order for joinder does not
require the applicant to prove that the commonality in issues and parties means
that the disposition of one action will necessarily dispose of the issues in
the other:
Liu
at para. 3;
Peel Financial Holdings Ltd. v. Western
Delta Lands Partnership
,
2003 BCSC 784 (B.C. S.C.)
[
Peel
] at paras.

27-32
.

[40]      Master
Keighley has described the test as "will the order make sense in the
circumstances":
Sohal Estate v. Argitos
,
2010 BCSC 916 (B.C. S.C.)

at para.
22
.

Waiver of the Implied Undertaking

[
62
]

Justice Barrow concisely the essential elements
of this undertaking in
Insurance Corp. of British Columbia v. Titanich
,

2010 BCSC 403
:

[13]      In
Juman v. Doucette
(Litigation Guardian of) v. Wee Watch Day Care Systems Inc.
, [2008] 1
S.C.R. 157,
2008 SCC 8 (S.C.C.)
[hereinafter
Juman
], Binnie J. addressed
the scope of the implied undertaking and its underlying rationale. At para. 4,
he wrote:

[4]        Thus the rule is that both
documentary and oral information obtained on discovery, including information
thought by one of the parties to disclose some sort of criminal conduct, is
subject to the implied undertaking. It is not to be used
by the other parties

except for the purpose of that litigation, unless and until the scope of the
undertaking is varied by a court order or other judicial order or a situation
of immediate and serious danger emerges.

…

[14]      The
rationale for the rule is, in part, to promote complete and candid oral and
documentary discovery which, in turn, advances the orderly and effective
administration of justice. It does that by providing the litigant making
discovery with some confidence that the material produced will be used only for
the purpose of securing justice in that proceeding.

[
63
]

Juman
itself
provides further practical guidance on the circumstances under which it will be
waived:

[35]      …For example, where discovery
material in one action is sought to be used in another action with the same or
similar parties and the same or similar issues, the prejudice to the examinee
is virtually non-existent and leave will generally be granted…

[36]      On the other hand, courts have
generally not favoured attempts to use the discovered material for an
extraneous purpose, or for an action wholly unrelated to the purposes of the
proceeding in which discovery was obtained in the absence of some compelling
public interest…

[38]      As stated,
the onus in each
case will be on the applicant to demonstrate a superior public interest in
disclosure, and the court will be mindful that an undertaking should only be
set aside in exceptional circumstances

[Emphasis added]

Mr. Mason

[
64
]

He focused his submissions on the suitability of these two matters
being heard together, treating the conversion of the Mansion House petition to
an action simply as a procedural step that is necessary to accomplish that goal.

[
65
]

He argues that his action and Mansion House’s petition are so
factually interwoven that a joint trial is appropriate. Crucially, the parties
are the same in both, despite the naming of the directors in the action, and
the punitive fines and contraventions of the House Rules that form the basis of
the oppression remedy he seeks (which I have ordered must be dealt with by a
petition) are also the basis of Mansion House’s petition to end his tenancy.
Further, if the oppression remedy is successful, the court will have a wide
discretion to address the conduct, including by varying or setting aside
resolutions that Mansion House is seeking to enforce.

[
66
]

Maintaining separate hearings creates a real danger that Mansion
House could succeed in having Mr. Mason give up possession and forfeit his
shares, only for him to demonstrate in a subsequent proceeding that its actions
in doing so were improper.

[
67
]

Mr. Mason also points out that the minimal prejudice cause by
delaying the hearing of Mansion House’s petition to schedule a joint trial
would be more than compensated for by being able to pursue joint pre-trial
discovery procedures, and ultimately only having to hold one hearing for both
proceedings.

[
68
]

Assuming his action proceeds together with the converted petition,
he also seeks waiver of the implied undertaking with respect to the
examinations for discovery, documents and admissions in the previous actions
between the parties, as well as in the converted petition action. In essence he
requires these materials to show the past actions of Mansion House, including
previous admissions of improper actions by board members, to advance his oppression
claim. For example, there was an admission on behalf of Mansion House in his
previous actions that the House Rules were changed in 2016 solely in order to
obtain a set of keys to Mr. Mason’s unit from him, which is an element of
his subsequent alleged breaches of those rules.

[
69
]

He points out, as I have previously summarized, that the Supreme
Court of Canada held in
Juman

that the prejudice arising from a waiver
when the same parties are involved in both actions is virtually non-existent. On
the other hand, if the waiver is not granted in this case, Mansion House will
essentially hide behind it to shield its conduct from appropriate review.

Mansion House

[
70
]

In contrast, Mansion House’s submissions focus on the
inappropriateness of converting its petition. It stresses that the petition
seeks orders that Mr. Mason wrongfully holds possession because his lease was
validly terminated in July of 2019. The only relevant time frame for that
purpose is between October 2018 and June 2019, when he is said to have breached
the House Rules and the terms of his lease – the alleged grounds for the
termination.

[
71
]

Most importantly, Mansion House says that the validity of the
termination has been partly determined by Skolrood J.’s order setting its
petition for the hearing pursuant to s.19 of the
CTA
.

[
72
]

Relying on
The Owners, Strata Plan VIS2030 v.
Ocean Park Towers Ltd
.,
2014 BCSC 264
, at paras.
14 and 21
, Mansion House
says that by succeeding in having the petition ordered to a hearing, it has
established a
prima facie
case, and that Mr. Mason now bears the
onus of showing why he should not be compelled to vacate. What is particularly
significant for our purposes is that the judge in
Ocean Park
declined to
order the matter to the trial list even though the respondent had also brought
an action alleging that the termination of the lease was invalid:

[21]      The petitioner contends that the
whole point of the summary proceedings under the
Commercial Tenancy Act

is to avoid the extensive costs associated with a trial. At a hearing of the
petition the burden is upon the tenant to show cause why it ought not to be
compelled to vacate the premises. The landlord is seeking to uphold the
termination. The civil claim advanced by the tenant seeks a declaration that
the termination was invalid.

[22]      A
hearing of the petition will resolve the basic issue. It will determine whether
the tenant is in breach of the lease or not. If it is, then that is the end of
the matter. If it is not, then that is also the end of the matter. If the
latter determination is made, the tenant could bring action for damages but
that would be a discrete issue fairly easily resolved.

[
73
]

That was also the outcome in
Broadway-Herb
Property Inc. v. Renegade Productions Inc
.,
2019 BCSC 1693
, in which it was
held that:

[37]      I do not consider that this
matter, which relates solely to the possession of the Premises, should be
referred to the trial list. None of the case law provided to me by Renegade
relates to the conversion of a petition for a writ of possession brought under
the
CTA
. The decision of our Court of Appeal in
Robertson
does
not say that all petitions are required to be converted to trials when there is
any arguable factual or legal defence raised. While the rules provide for
discretion in that regard, it is by no means a requirement. Many legal and
factual matters are determined by petition, and this Court has discretion in
considering what, if any, trial processes ought to apply to a petition
proceeding.

[38]      In
this case, I am able resolve the possession issue as between the parties on the
basis of the materials before me in a way that does not require the resolution
of disputed facts. I am satisfied that the
CTA
sets out a deliberate
summary process for determination of possession of a commercial premises, and
that this matter should proceed summarily. A determination of damages under the
lease as between the parties may well require a trial, but at this point, no
such action has been filed. If an action is filed, it may proceed regardless of
whether the Landlord or Renegade has possession of the Premises.

[
74
]

Mansion House argue that there should be a similar result here. In
particular there are no bona fide triable issues that would require a trial, as
opposed to the summary proceedings envisioned under the
CTA
. The
existing affidavits provide an ample evidentiary basis to resolve the
evidentiary issues and it is also unnecessary to resolve the credibility of any

have the authority to terminate his lease for breaches of the House Rules, but
he does not contest the subsequent termination of his lease by a vote of the

only a dispute about the legal effect of the facts surrounding the termination.

[
75
]

In addition, Mansion House notes that Mr. Mason’s affidavits do not
actually identify additional evidence that would be required if the petition
were heard as a trial, only his wish to engage in the available pre-trial

expedition. In any event, it will be possible for Mr. Mason to obtain such
procedures by an application pursuant to s. 22-1(4) without the petition
being converted, and Rule 16-1(18) establishes that any other of the
Rules

may be applied to a petition.

[
76
]

On the question of a joint trial of both matters, Mansion House
questions whether there are actually any common or interwoven claims here. In
the petition it seeks the narrow remedies of vacant possession of the unit,
forfeiture of Mr. Mason’s shares, the right to sell them, and a lien on
any proceeds of the sale. This is in stark contrast to the various broad claims
advanced in his action. It is also highly relevant that Mansion House’s
petition is at a much more advanced stage than the action. It was set for a
hearing in March of 2020 (which could not be held because these applications
had not been concluded), while the action has not even had its pleadings
finalized yet, as the first application demonstrated.

[
77
]

Should it become necessary to consider it, Mansion House submits
that the required public interest in the exceptional measure of waiving the
implied undertaking has not yet been shown. There have only been general

(but not insignificant) consideration, it points out that he has not sought the
position or consent of the individuals whose discovery evidence would actually
be accessed by such a measure.

Discussion

[
78
]

I agree with Mansion House that the question of whether its petition
should be put on the trial list is a discrete issue that must be determined
before the question of hearing it together with Mr. Mason’s action arises, and
that the former question is not subsumed in the latter.

[
79
]

Fundamentally, the question is whether Mr. Mason has raised a bona
fide triable issue on the petition, as it was defined in
Saputo
. As in
the case of an application for summary judgment, I must conduct a limited
review of the evidence, without weighing it (
Richter Estate v. Richter
,

2018 BCCA 238
, at para.
29
), and determine whether he is “bound to lose” on the
issue that he seeks to raise.

[
80
]

When engaging in this determination, it is important to keep in mind
that the question of whether the matter can be decided on the basis of
affidavit evidence, with respect to issues such as credibility, only arises in
the context of a summary trial – the relevant question on whether a petition
goes to the trial list is the presence a triable issue:
C.M.R. v. L.F.R.
,

2019 BCCA 371
at para.11.

[
81
]

I should say that I do not find
Ocean Park and Broadway-Herb
,
the cases relied on by Mansion house to be determinative of this question, as
Mansion House suggests.
Ocean Park
was resolved on the question of
whether a
prima facie
case of overholding had been made out by the
landlord – the petitioner’s counsel conceded that the matter should go on the
trial list if it had not.
Broadway-Herb
did not directly apply the test in

Saputo
, only the general statement in the underlying authority of
Robertson

that a petition does not have to go on the trial list whenever an arguable
factual or legal defence has been advanced.

[
82
]

However, Ocean Park does make the useful point that there can be
situations in which a petition will resolve an issue that is common to another
proceeding that the opposing party wishes to have joined.

[
83
]

Mansion House’s petition seeks to uphold the termination of Mr.
Mason’s lease pursuant to directors’ resolution in May of 2019, followed by a
shareholders’ resolution to the same effect that June. These were based on his
frequent violations of the House Rules (which were found to be a breach of a
material term of the lease), his failure to correct the conduct that had
resulted in fines for the violations, and to pay those fines. The question is
whether Mr. Mason’s claim that these procedures were carried out in a manner
that was unfair to him are “bound to lose”

[
84
]

In answering this question, one must keep additional two points in
mind.

[
85
]

First, what is a triable issue is defined by the issues in the
petition itself, not in any related proceeding. This is not Mr. Mason’s
application pursuant to the
BCA
for a finding that Mansion House’s
actions towards him were significantly unfair. The directors’ actions are
relevant to this petition to the extent that they could undermine the basis on
which his lease was terminated. If he were successful in proving his oppression
claims, a court might well consider reviewing the resolutions and/or the
underlying house rules and purported violations. But the fact that he is
pursuing those remedies in another proceeding does not in itself create a
triable issue on the petition.

[
86
]

With one exception, Mr. Mason’s extensive
allegations of wrongdoing by the board in his notice of civil claim and affidavits
- including its campaign against him, its violation of the spirit of the
settlement agreement and its creation of House Rules intended to create more violations
- do not address the actual validity of those resolutions, in terms of how they
were proposed and enacted. The exception is found in paragraph 46 of the notice
of civil claim:

On June 20,
2019, the meeting was held. In this meeting, the Board falsely stated that the
Plaintiff owed strata fines, was in breach of a number of rules and was
uncooperative with respect to “his violations”. The Board did not inform the
shareholders that the Board had, since around 2002, engaged in a protracted and
litigious campaign of harassment against the Plaintiff or that the alleged
“house rules” had been passed only for the purpose of imposing fines on the
Plaintiff, and, it seems, facilitating a means by which the Board would purport
to eject the Plaintiff from his home.

[
87
]

While this assertion does address the process by which the
shareholders’ resolution was obtained, it is not clear to me that it actually
raises a triable issue of fact. Based on the PowerPoint slides in the
application material, which were apparently shown to the attendees at the
extraordinary general meeting, and the accompanying resolution, it seems
apparent that the directors did not inform the shareholders of any campaign by
them against Mr. Mason. In other words, that fact is not disputed, and to the
extent that it could undermine the validity of the termination his lease, a
trial is not necessary to resolve that issue.

[
88
]

The second point is that the existence of a triable issue is based
on a limited review of the evidence, not the pleadings. As Mansion House points
out, there is currently no evidence beyond Mr. Mason’s bare assertions (and the
one excerpt from a previous examination for discovery in which a representative
of Mansion House says the House Rules regarding keys was directed at him, which
is not necessarily improper) that the rules that led to the accumulated fines
were improperly motivated. I agree that it would not be appropriate to put the
matter on the trial list only so that he can seek to obtain such evidence. As
Mansion House also points out, he could seek to employ pre-trial discovery
procedures to that end in the context of the existing petition.

[
89
]

His affidavits do contain some factual disputes
about the circumstances underlying the incidents for which he was fined, but the
affidavits are mainly focused on the legitimacy of the board having fined him
for things that he acknowledges occurred, based on his general assertion of an
improper purpose. It is not clear that any of the factual disputes that have
been put forward at this point would be capable in themselves of undermining
the validity of the termination resolutions, by showing an improper motivation
for the underlying disciplinary action. In other words, the available evidence
does not provide a basis on which a judge could go behind those disciplinary
actions. As Justice Griffin explained in
Ghag v. Ghag
,
2021 BCCA 106
:

44        … [E]ach
side must put its best foot forward at the hearing.…[A] self-serving affidavit
is not sufficient in itself to create a triable issue in the absence of
detailed facts and supporting evidence:
Guarantee Co. of North America v.
Gordon Capital Corp.
,
1999 CanLII 664 (SCC)
, [1999] 3 S.C.R. 423 at para.
31

[
90
]

Thus, I find that on the current record that Mr. Mason is bound to
lose on his general assertion that he has been dealt with in a substantially
unfair manner by Mansion House, which is the issue that relates to the relief
that Mansion House seeks in its petition, and that therefore there is no
triable issue that would require the petition to be transferred to the trial
list. He is certainly entitled to raise the conduct of Mansion House and the
directors towards him in the context of resisting its petition, as was found in

Ocean Park
, but there is currently no proper basis on which to convert
it into an action.

[
91
]

This conclusion makes it strictly unnecessary to
consider whether the petition and the action should be heard together. Had it
been necessary to do so, and leaving aside the fact that I have already decided
that the oppression claims need to be heard as a petition, I would have
concluded that while there are common parties and issues, at least in relation
to the oppression claim and Mansion House’s petition, it would inappropriate to
delay the hearing of the petition, which is at a much more advanced stage, when
Mr. Mason can raise any concerns about the board’s actions in the hearing of
the Mansion House petition that he could have raised when seeking the
oppression remedy. Given the relevance of the same alleged conduct that would
underlie his oppression proceeding,
I find the possibility of inconsistent decisions between the two
proceedings to be minimal.

[
92
]

In view of these conclusions, it is also unnecessary to consider the
issue of waiving the implied undertaking.

Costs

[
93

In
Crema v. Apple Inc.
,
2020 BCSC 1767
, Justice Matthews
permitted the plaintiff to amend the notice of civil claim to make reference to
the
Criminal Code
provisions relating to unauthorized use of a computer
and mischief to data, in a case in which a form of electronic trespass was
being alleged. Matthews J. found that the provisions “may provide a useful
